subject: fabergeEgg

Category: Object.
Subject: jewelled egg opening to reveal a tiny automaton.

reasoning:

I'm keeping the rig simple with a few key joints -- a base, a lid hinge for opening, and maybe a rotating turntable -- since this is more of an object than a creature, so it doesn't need a full skeleton. Now I'm working out the proportions in meters, with the closed egg around 0.14m tall and the whole stand assembly roughly 0.2m.

I'm defining the egg's silhouette as a lathed profile, narrower at the top than the bottom, then figuring out where to split the shell -- probably around 62% up from the base, like a classic surprise egg. The lower half becomes a shell with outer and inner walls (so it has real thickness and a floor the automaton sits on), while the upper half becomes the lid, hinged at the back rim and swung open about 100 degrees, topped with a small finial like a gold pearl or crown.

I'm working out the rotation math for the hinge: rotating around the X-axis by roughly -110 degrees so the lid's front edge lifts up while the dome swings back and down, keeping the opening motion anatomically sensible relative to the hinge line at the back rim.

I'll settle on roughly -100° instead, keeping everything within bounds. I'll set this up as a joint-based hinge: build the lid geometry in its closed position first, attached to a bone, then apply the pose rotation afterward.

Now checking the rotation direction convention — a positive degree value should tip a forward-pointing bone downward, which matches my derivation, so the pivot and axis setup are consistent.

Turning to the design details, I'm thinking of a Fabergé-style palette with translucent enamel guilloché in jewel tones like raspberry and royal blue.

For the lower egg half, I'm leaning toward deep sapphire enamel with a guilloché sunburst, painted procedurally using the lathe height and angle parameters — mixing light and dark blue based on a sine-wave interference pattern to simulate the engraved guilloché texture, then layering gold bands and lattice work on top.

Now I'm figuring out the gold ornamentation: a rim band plus meridian ribs swept along the egg's profile at different azimuth angles, offset slightly outward from the surface using the same profile function, then repeated symmetrically on both the lid and lower half.

I'll write a helper function to generate ring positions and place parts directly with explicit bone references, sticking to well-documented API calls rather than relying on uncertain behaviors. For the automaton figure, I'm deciding on a small harlequin or ballerina doll with a decorated head sphere and raised arms for a richer visual read than a generic songbird.

Now I'm sketching the ballerina's tutu as a ring of extruded enamel petals, mounted on a gear-driven turntable using the clockwork kit's gear train, plus a winding key at the back of the egg stand for authenticity. Then I'm working out component dimensions in meters: the egg's overall closed height, and a gold pedestal stand with a flared foot disc, stem, and cup to hold the egg, supported by three curving rococo-style gold legs sweeping up from the base.

I'm refining the pedestal with a lathed base and flared stem leading to a cup at the egg's resting point, plus four scrolled legs curving from the foot ring up to that cup. Then I'm working out the egg's geometric profile -- center height, semi-height, bottom and top points -- to figure out total model height once the lid opens and the automaton rises, parameterizing the egg's curve from top to bottom.

Now I'm calculating where to cut the egg into lower and upper shells, slightly above the equator so the lower shell is larger, then checking the rim radius at that cut and how much interior depth the lower shell gives for the automaton to stand inside with its legs just below the opening.

I need to separate the outer enamel shell from the inner velvet lining as two distinct lathe shapes so they can have different colors, since a single lathe outline can't easily carry two materials.

Simplifying: I'll do a shell lathe with outer enamel paint for the outer surface and wall thickness, then add a slightly inset lining lathe for the interior (cream silk material) that sits just inside the inner wall so it visually covers it without z-fighting, since the closer surface to the viewer wins. The lining's top edge will stop just short of the rim, and I'm considering an ivory satin or pale pink tone for the interior color.

For segment counts, I'm using 24 lathe segments for the egg shape with around 14 profile points per side to keep curvature smooth while avoiding sharp creases. I'm working out the profile point ordering carefully -- starting at the bottom axis point, tracing up the outer wall to the rim, then back down the inner wall to the bottom -- making sure the path never self-intersects and that x stays non-negative throughout.

The slight slope at the rim edge is acceptable, and closing the outline along the axis back to the first point works fine with duplicates dropped—no sharp marking needed since smoothing is zero, and the point count stays well under 512. I'm setting the lathe axis to the default vertical orientation at the origin, with y measured relative to that point.

Now I'm working out the joint hierarchy: a root "base" joint, a "lid" joint parented to base at the hinge position with a hinge role, and other joints like a spinning turntable, dancer figures, left/right arms, a head, and possibly a winding key—deciding which ones need explicit roles versus which can skip that field.

I'm figuring out interior clearance inside the egg shell to fit a small gear train and turntable mechanism—calculating the available radius at a given height using the egg's curvature, then sizing a deck around 0.04 radius to hold a center dancer platform and small surrounding gears.

Working out the gear train layout: setting a vertical axis, making the center gear double as the turntable the dancer stands on, and spacing smaller meshing gears around it based on tooth counts and module size to get proper pitch distances.

I'm checking gear positions in the train to confirm none overlap, computing distances and angular placements for gear1 and gear2 relative to gear0 to verify spacing stays within the compound shift footprint.
